titre: What your trash says that you wouldn't
accroche: By digging through Tucson's garbage, archaeologists measured the gap between what people say and what they do
contenu_vulgarise:
Archaeology almost always deals with people who can no longer be questioned. So it developed a particular skill: reading behavior from what it leaves behind.

In 1973, William Rathje decided to turn that skill on the present. His team at the University of Arizona began sorting through Tucson's garbage using the protocols applied at an ancient site: sorting by category, weighing, recording by household, without ever meeting the residents.

At the same time, interviewers had the same households fill out questionnaires about their consumption.

## Two measurements that don't match

The value of the setup lies in the comparison. For the same household, there is what it says it consumes and what it throws away.

The two do not overlap.

Reported alcohol consumption is markedly lower than what the containers reveal. The measured gap is considerable. Food waste is the reverse: the households surveyed claim they throw away almost nothing, while the garbage shows that a notable share of the food they buy ends up in the trash intact.

None of these gaps requires deliberate lying. People underestimate what they disapprove of, forget what is routine, and remember the intention rather than the act. The questionnaire records the image a household has of itself; the waste records what it did.

## What the project overturned

Excavations later carried out in deep landfills contradicted several certainties of the time.

The share of materials reputed to overrun landfills turned out to be far smaller than supposed, while paper took up considerable volumes. Above all, the expected degradation did not happen: newspapers dug up after decades were still readable, food scraps still recognizable. A compacted landfill is an environment poor in oxygen and water. It preserves rather than decomposes.

## The reversal

The project founded a practice, garbology, but its main contribution is methodological, and it concerns all the social sciences.

Asking people about their behavior measures a statement. Collecting what they leave behind measures the behavior. Both are data, but they are not about the same object, and it is unwise to treat the first as a substitute for the second.

There is some reassurance here for the archaeologist of the past, incidentally. The sources are mute, and archaeologists have long experienced that as a handicap. The Tucson garbage suggests the opposite: a society that can no longer tell its own story is a society you can observe without a filter.

repere.texte: Tucson households say they throw away almost nothing, yet their garbage shows that about 15% of the solid food they buy goes into the trash. Alcohol consumption, meanwhile, is heavily underreported.
repere.source: Rathje, “The Garbage Project & The Archaeology of Us,” Encyclopaedia Britannica Yearbook of Science and the Future

carte.punch: Asking people measures a statement. Digging through their garbage measures behavior.
carte.idee: Since 1973, the Garbage Project has dug through Tucson's trash as if it were an ancient site. The result: alcohol is heavily underreported, and households that claim to waste nothing throw away about 15% of the food they buy.

quiz.question: What did the comparison of questionnaires and garbage mainly establish?
choix: That the people surveyed deliberately lie about their consumption
That landfills decompose waste much faster than was thought
That a statement and a behavior are two different things to measure
That food waste is lower than households estimate
quiz.explication: The gap does not imply any lying: people underestimate what they disapprove of and forget what is routine. The questionnaire measures the image a household has of itself; the garbage measures what it does. The excavations also showed the opposite of the other two options: landfills preserve, and actual waste exceeds the reported estimate.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the excavations later carried out in deep landfills show?
choix: That waste decomposed there much faster than was believed at the time
That paper took up considerable volumes there, and that nothing degraded
That materials reputed to overrun landfills took up most of the volume
That households mostly dumped food scraps there, and little packaging
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The share of materials reputed to overrun landfills turned out to be far smaller than supposed, while paper took up considerable volumes. Newspapers dug up after decades were still readable: compacted, a landfill is poor in oxygen and water, and it preserves rather than decomposes.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does reported alcohol consumption compare with what the garbage reveals?
choix: It is markedly lower than what the discarded containers show
It is markedly higher than what the discarded containers show
It matches fairly closely what the discarded containers show
It could not be compared, because containers were excluded from the sorting
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Alcohol is heavily underreported, and the measured gap is considerable. Food waste goes the other way: households claim they throw away almost nothing, yet a notable share of the food they buy ends up in the trash intact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How did Rathje's team proceed in Tucson starting in 1973?
choix: It rode along with garbage collectors to question residents on their doorsteps
It installed cameras in kitchens to record actual behavior
It bought households' store receipts to reconstruct their purchases
It sorted and weighed the garbage household by household, never meeting the residents
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The protocol is that of an ancient site: sorting by category, weighing, recording by household, with no contact with the residents. In parallel, interviewers had the same households fill out questionnaires about their consumption.
